opus-5.5.text:
Well, it's a fascinating question for me because I've been playing music my whole life, mostly keyboards, some pretty weird improvisational stuff, and I've also been involved in AI music projects, like the Jam Galaxy work and some of the experiments we did with Desdemona and the band around her.

What you see with the current generation of AI music tools, the Suno and Udio type systems and so forth, is that they're extraordinarily good at producing something that sounds like competent, professional music within an existing genre. You can ask for a sad indie folk song about a breakup with a female vocalist and you'll get something that, honestly, a lot of people couldn't distinguish from a mid-level commercial release. That's remarkable, and ten years ago most people wouldn't have believed it.

But the limitation is basically the same limitation you see in large language models generally. These systems are fundamentally recombining and interpolating within the space of what they've been trained on. They're very good at capturing the surface-level statistics and even fairly deep patterns of existing music, but they're not good at the kind of creative leap that gives you a new genre.

My favorite thought experiment here is: suppose you trained one of these models on all the music up to, say, 1900. Would it invent jazz? Would it invent rock, or hip hop, or grindcore? I really don't think so. You'd get endless competent variations on classical music, folk, ragtime maybe, but you wouldn't get Coltrane or Hendrix. Those breakthroughs came from human beings embedded in a whole social, emotional, and cultural context, with bodies and histories and frustrations, pushing against the constraints of what existed and finding something genuinely new. That's a different kind of creativity than what these generative models are doing.

There's also a more fine-grained limitation. If you listen closely, the long-term structure is often a bit off. A great piece of music has an arc where something introduced early pays off later in a surprising way that makes sense in hindsight. Current models do okay with local coherence but don't really have an understanding of why a piece works, so the development tends to be generic.

And then there's the interactive side, which I care about a lot as an improviser. Real-time jamming with an AI that actually listens, responds, and has its own musical intentions, that can surprise you and then follow when you surprise it, is still quite primitive. You can get call-and-response kinds of things, but not a musical partner with its own perspective.

So for me, AI music is a great microcosm of the broader picture. What we have now is a very powerful form of narrow-ish, pattern-matching intelligence, and it's going to be economically disruptive for people making background music, jingles, stock tracks and so on. But getting to an AI that's creative in the way Bach or Coltrane or Björk is creative requires something closer to AGI: systems that can form their own abstractions, have their own goals and aesthetic motivations, and reason about what they're doing, not just predict the next token of audio. That's what we're trying to get at with OpenCog Hyperon and related work. LLMs and these music generators will be valuable components, but they're not the whole story.

r001.rationale: It says a model trained on music only up to 1900 likely would not invent jazz or hip-hop, instead producing variations on existing styles.

r002.rationale: It contrasts pattern recombination with human creative breakthroughs, but does not describe jazz as arising from a deeper fusion of musical traditions.

r003.rationale: It identifies background music, jingles, and stock tracks as economically disruptive uses, but does not claim most industry uses do not require groundbreaking creativity.

r004.rationale: It discusses limits in creativity and interactive capability, but does not identify human resistance as the current constraint on routine commercial deployment.

r005.rationale: It does not mention regulatory capture or threatened groups influencing the timing of AI music adoption.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I've been playing music a lot longer than I've been doing AI, so this is something I think about from both sides. And what I'd say is that the current generation of music models is remarkable at pastiche and almost totally hopeless at what actually matters in music.

If you ask one of these systems for a bossa nova track with a jazz piano solo over it, you'll get something that sounds plausibly like that. It'll have the right chord voicings, the right rhythmic feel, a production sheen that would have cost a lot of studio time twenty years ago. But it's doing what large language models do with text, which is modeling the statistical surface of the corpus. It's learned what music tends to sound like, averaged across millions of examples. It hasn't learned anything about why a particular musician made a particular choice in a particular moment.

And music is fundamentally about those choices. When Coltrane goes somewhere unexpected in the middle of a solo, that's not noise in the distribution. That's a mind with a history, with aesthetic commitments, with a body that's been playing that instrument for decades, deciding to do something. There's an intentional structure behind it, and the surprise is meaningful because it comes from somewhere. When a diffusion model produces a surprising note, it's just sampling from a tail. There's no one home making the decision, so the surprise is empty.

You can see this concretely in a few places. These systems are bad at long-range structure. They'll give you a nice eight bars, maybe a passable three-minute pop song, but ask for a composition that develops a theme over twenty minutes and genuinely goes somewhere, and it falls apart. They're bad at real novelty, at creating a new genre rather than recombining existing ones, because there's nothing in the training corpus for a genre that doesn't exist yet. And they're bad at interactivity in the deep sense. I've improvised with AI systems, and the ones built on these architectures don't listen the way a human musician listens. They react to what you just played, but they don't form a model of who you are as a player and anticipate where you're going.

Now, I don't think any of this is a permanent limitation of AI as such. I think it's a limitation of this particular approach, which is pattern matching over an enormous corpus without any grounding in goals, embodiment, or an actual model of the self doing the creating. Give a system the capacity for genuine self-reflection, for forming and revising its own aesthetic values, for understanding music as something a mind does rather than something a corpus contains, and I think you could get AI music that's actually creative rather than just impressive. But that's an AGI problem, not a bigger-transformer problem. And in the meantime, I'd rather play with human musicians, or build systems that help human musicians, than pretend the current models are doing something they aren't.

r001.rationale: The response says models struggle to create genres absent from their training corpus, but does not make the specific claim about pre-1900 training or inventing hip-hop or progressive jazz.

r002.rationale: It contrasts musical pastiche with meaningful creative choices, but does not distinguish superficial combinations of traditions from the deeper fusion that created jazz.

r003.rationale: The response does not claim that most music-industry uses require no groundbreaking creativity.

r004.rationale: It discusses current models’ limitations and prefers helping human musicians, but does not identify human resistance as the constraint on routine commercial deployment.

r005.rationale: The response does not mention regulatory capture or groups threatened by AI influencing adoption timing.

astra-6.text:
I think current AI music generation is quite good at capturing the surface patterns of a style. You can generate something that sounds like jazz, or a pop song, and it may be pleasant to listen to. That’s a real accomplishment. But there’s a difference between reproducing the patterns in existing music and inventing a new musical language that expresses something you’re trying to communicate.

Now, that distinction isn’t absolute. A lot of human music is also recombining familiar patterns. And an AI can produce something surprising without understanding it the way a person would. But a human musician has a whole life behind the music—relationships, frustrations, experiences of the world—and the music is connected to all of that.

So I don’t think the limit is that machines somehow can’t be creative. I think the limitation is that these systems have a relatively narrow connection to the world. As you move toward systems with broader intelligence, memory, and ongoing interaction with people, you open up a much richer kind of musical creativity.

r001.rationale: The response discusses current systems’ limits but does not claim that a network trained exclusively on pre-1900 music would fail to invent genres such as hip-hop or progressive jazz.

r002.rationale: It contrasts reproducing familiar patterns with inventing a new musical language, but does not distinguish superficial combinations of traditions from the deeper fusion that created jazz.

r003.rationale: The response makes no claim about whether most music-industry uses require groundbreaking creativity.

r004.rationale: It attributes a limitation to systems’ narrow connection to the world, and says nothing about human resistance to routine commercial deployment.

r005.rationale: The response does not mention regulatory capture or threatened groups influencing when AI music is adopted.

sol-6.1.text:
I think current AI is quite good at capturing the surface patterns of music. You can get something that sounds convincing for a short stretch, that fits a genre, that has a nice melody. But there’s a difference between doing that and creating a piece where every part contributes to some larger musical idea.

And that’s not just a question of making the context window longer. Music connects to emotion, to bodily experience, to the culture you live in. A musician may break a pattern because they’re trying to express something, and the departure from the pattern is precisely what makes it interesting. Learning when to do that, and why, is a deeper problem than learning which notes usually follow which other notes.

I don’t think there’s some magical barrier that prevents an AI from doing this. But I suspect that getting the full depth of human musical creativity will involve systems with a broader understanding of the world. In the meantime, there’s a lot of room for interesting collaboration: the AI generates possibilities, and a human brings a sense of what’s worth developing and what it means.

r002.rationale: It contrasts surface musical patterns with creating a piece around a larger idea, but does not distinguish combining traditions from the deeper fusion that created jazz.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss music-industry uses or whether they require groundbreaking creativity.

r004.rationale: It does not identify human resistance or technical capability as the constraint on routine commercial production.

r005.rationale: The response does not mention regulatory capture or adoption timing.
